A reviewer can replay the duplicate request and see the second call return the first result, not a second write.
backend-request-response.unlock: Your contract validates input before it touches state, authorizes before it acts, persists exactly once under retry, and returns a typed envelope for both success and failure.
backend-request-response.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'handle the request' if your handler writes to the database before validation and auth pass, or if a retried POST creates a second row. A handler that is correct only on the happy path is a demo, not a contract. The contract is the behavior under bad input, wrong caller, and retry.

backend-request-response.text: A customer taps 'Place order' on a flaky connection, the spinner hangs, they tap again — and the warehouse ships two. The handler did exactly what the code said on each call; nobody wrote down what it must do when the same request arrives twice.

Every backend endpoint is a promise: given this request, under this caller, I will change state exactly this much and return exactly this shape — even when the input is wrong, the caller is not allowed, or the network retries. This lesson turns that promise into the first artifact every later module (queues, jobs, observability, compatibility) builds on.

backend-request-response.prompt: Your POST /orders handler works perfectly in every test. A client sends the same request twice because the first response timed out. What does your endpoint do — and is that a bug in the client or in you? Answer before reading on.
backend-request-response.reveal: It is your bug. A timeout means the client never learned whether the write happened, so a retry is correct behavior — the contract has to absorb it. A handler that creates a second order on the second call is missing idempotency: a key that lets the server recognize 'I already did this' and return the FIRST result. The request/response contract is not 'parse and write'; it is what happens on the second, wrong, or unauthorized copy of the same request.

backend-request-response.intro: Writing the handler, one boundary at a time. Trace one complete boundary decision before changing the handler.
steps: Validate before state: Parse against a schema first. A bad shape returns 400 and never reaches the database — the request never gets to touch state until it is well-formed.

Authorize the caller: Authentication (who are you) then authorization (may you act on THIS resource). 401 vs 403 is the auth boundary: missing identity vs forbidden action. This is OWASP API1 — broken object-level authorization — caught at the door.
Require the idempotency key: A state-changing request with no idempotency key cannot be made safe under retry. Demand it; reject with 400 if absent.
The exactly-once check: Inside the transaction, first look up the key. If it was already processed, replay the FIRST response — no second write. This is the line that absorbs the double-tap.

One transaction, write + key together: Insert the order AND save the idempotency record in the SAME transaction so they commit or roll back as a unit. Saving the key outside the txn would let a crash double-write.
Typed envelope, success and rollback: 201 with a typed body on success; any throw rolls the whole transaction back, leaving no partial order. The response shape is the contract clients code against.

storyboard.say: It starts with a tap. The client fires a POST to /orders and the API gateway receives it as the single entry point.
The gateway routes it inward, but nothing touches state yet. First the handler checks whether the request shape is even valid.
Shape is fine, so we ask a second question: is this caller allowed to do this at all? Authorization gates the action before it happens.
Now the crucial gate. The idempotency check looks up the request key to decide: is this a brand-new order, or one we've already seen?
A new key means act. Only now do we open one transaction and commit the write to Postgres exactly once.
The retry story: the spinner hung, they tapped again, same key. We replay the first result instead of writing a second order.
Both paths converge on one typed envelope. Success or failure, the endpoint keeps its promise: state changes only after the gates pass, and only once.

backend-request-response.text: Grounded in OWASP API Security Top 10: the #1 risk is broken object-level authorization — a handler that authenticates ('you have a valid token') but never authorizes ('this token may act on THIS order'). The senior tell is the line `caller.id !== body.customerId → 403`: identity is not permission, and the contract checks both before it writes anything.

backend-request-response.question: A reviewer asks for the exact evidence that your endpoint is exactly-once, not just happy-path. What do you point to?
options: The unit test showing one valid request creates one order.

A replay test: the same request with the same Idempotency-Key sent twice — the second returns the first result with zero new rows — plus the rollback test showing a mid-transaction failure leaves no partial order.
The fact that the handler compiles and the schema type-checks.
A comment in the code that says // idempotent.
backend-request-response.explanation: Exactly-once is a behavior under retry and failure, so the proof has to exercise retry and failure: a duplicate-submit replay that writes nothing the second time, and a rollback test proving a crash mid-transaction leaves no partial state. The happy-path test (1), a clean compile (3), and a comment (4) all only confirm the path that was never in question.

backend-request-response.title: Implement an exactly-once POST /orders handler with an Idempotency-Key
backend-request-response.summary: Complete the handle_create_order function so the request/response cycle validates, authenticates, authorizes, and enforces an exactly-once idempotency contract, then run it in the browser to print the request log.
backend-request-response.starter:
# Lab: Exactly-once POST /orders handler with an Idempotency-Key contract.
#
# You are implementing the request/response cycle for a state-changing endpoint.
# Each request is a dict. Implement handle_create_order(req) so it returns a
# (status, body) tuple and enforces this contract IN THIS ORDER:
#
#   1. Validate body: req["body"] must have "customer_id" (int) and
#      "amount" (int > 0). Otherwise return (400, {"ok": False, "error": "INVALID_BODY"}).
#   2. Authenticate: req["token"] must equal VALID_TOKEN.
#      Otherwise (401, {"ok": False, "error": "UNAUTHENTICATED"}).
#   3. Authorize: TOKEN_OWNER must equal body["customer_id"].
#      Otherwise (403, {"ok": False, "error": "FORBIDDEN"}).
#   4. Require req["idempotency_key"] to be non-empty.
#      Otherwise (400, {"ok": False, "error": "IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REQUIRED"}).
#   5. Exactly-once: if the key was already used, return the SAME stored
#      response and DO NOT create another order. Otherwise create a new order
#      (ids start at 1 and increment), store its response under the key, and
#      return (200, {"ok": True, "order_id": <id>, "amount": <amount>}).

TOKEN_OWNER = 42          # the id the valid token belongs to
VALID_TOKEN = "secret-abc"

# Persistent state (shared across all requests in this run)
_idempotency_store = {}    # key -> (status, body)
_orders = {}               # order_id -> order
_next_id = [1]             # next order id to assign


def handle_create_order(req):
    # TODO: implement the contract above. Return (status:int, body:dict).
    raise NotImplementedError


# Fixed request sequence (do not edit)
REQUESTS = [
    {"token": "secret-abc", "idempotency_key": "k1",
     "body": {"customer_id": 42, "amount": 100}},
    {"token": "secret-abc", "idempotency_key": "k1",
     "body": {"customer_id": 42, "amount": 100}},
    {"token": "secret-abc", "idempotency_key": "k2",
     "body": {"customer_id": 42, "amount": 250}},
    {"token": "bad",        "idempotency_key": "k3",
     "body": {"customer_id": 42, "amount": 50}},
    {"token": "secret-abc", "idempotency_key": "k4",
     "body": {"customer_id": 7,  "amount": 50}},
    {"token": "secret-abc", "idempotency_key": "",
     "body": {"customer_id": 42, "amount": 50}},
    {"token": "secret-abc", "idempotency_key": "k5",
     "body": {"customer_id": 42, "amount": -5}},
]

for i, req in enumerate(REQUESTS, start=1):
    status, body = handle_create_order(req)
    print(f"req{i}: {status} {body['error'] if not body['ok'] else 'order=' + str(body['order_id'])}")

print(f"orders_created: {len(_orders)}")

resource-modeling.outcome: Take one state-changing endpoint (real or realistic — e.g. POST /orders) and model the resource: name the resource, its fields and invariants, the request/response contract, and the validation + authorization boundary every request must cross before it touches the database.
resource-modeling.proof: Section 1 of api_contract_and_failure_repair_packet.md: a named resource with typed fields, a request schema, a response schema, and the explicit validation + auth gate. A reviewer reads it and can send a malformed request and predict the exact rejection — status code, error shape, and which boundary caught it — without running your code.
resource-modeling.unlock: Your model names the resource, its invariants, the typed request/response contract, and the validation + auth boundary that guards the write path.
resource-modeling.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have 'modeled the resource' if your model is just a database table. A table is storage; a resource is the contract the outside world sees plus the invariants you defend. If the only thing you wrote down is columns, you skipped the boundary that actually protects the system.

resource-modeling.text: A POST /orders endpoint ships with no model — just a handler that trusts its input and inserts. Friday, a client double-clicks 'Pay', two identical requests race, and the database now holds two orders for one cart. Nobody modeled the resource, so nobody owned the invariant that should have made that impossible.

Every backend endpoint is a promise: this resource, these fields, these rules, enforced here. Resource modeling is where that promise is written down — Section 1 of the contract packet you carry through validation, authorization, persistence, and idempotency.

resource-modeling.prompt: Your handler does `db.orders.insert(request.body)` — it takes the JSON the client sent and writes it straight to the table. Before you optimize anything, what is wrong with that as a resource model? Answer before reading on.
resource-modeling.reveal: There is no model — there is a passthrough. The client, not you, decides the shape, and the client is untrusted external input. Nothing checks that `total` matches the line items, nothing rejects an extra `isAdmin: true` field, nothing confirms this user may create an order at all. A resource model is the layer that turns 'whatever the client sent' into 'a valid Order, owned by this caller, that satisfies my invariants' — and its absence is invisible until production sends you the request you never imagined.

resource-modeling.intro: Modeling the Order resource, one declaration at a time. Trace one complete boundary decision before changing the handler.
steps: The request schema: The resource's inbound shape, typed. The client may send these fields and only these — this is the contract, not a suggestion.

z.strictObject() — the field whitelist: Reject unknown fields. Without this, a client can append isAdmin: true or ownerId: <someone-else> and you'd silently persist it. In Zod 4 the idiomatic form is z.strictObject({...}); the older z.object({...}).strict() still works but is deprecated. Either way, this closes a mass-assignment hole (OWASP API3).

The invariant: A resource is more than its types: total must equal the sum of line items. Types can't express this; the invariant function can. A test that can only confirm the happy path never catches a tampered total — this can.

The response contract: What the resource looks like coming back — including ownerId, set by the server, never by the client. The outbound shape is part of the model, not an afterthought. (Zod 4: the ISO timestamp uses z.iso.datetime().)

resource-modeling.title: A resource is a contract + invariants + a boundary — not a table
resource-modeling.text: Name the resource and its typed fields, state the invariants that must always hold, define the request/response schemas the outside sees, and place the validation + authorization boundary the write must cross. The invariant: untrusted input becomes a valid, owned resource before it touches the store.

resource-modeling.title: The request crossing the resource boundary
resource-modeling.subtitle: Every state-changing request runs the same gauntlet: parse → validate the contract → check authorization → enforce invariants → persist. The validation and auth gates are the suspect path; an unvalidated write is the failure mode.

legend.label: the resource boundary — validation + auth gates
invariant enforcement + typed rejection
source of truth — reached only by a valid, owned write

storyboard.say: A client fires a state-changing request at the API handler — this is the promise the endpoint has to keep.
The handler parses the raw body first. Right now it's untrusted input — nothing here is known to be safe yet.
Gate one: validate against the schema. Wrong shape, missing fields, bad types — the request is rejected before it goes further.
If the shape is valid, it crosses to authorization — the second gate on the suspect path.
Gate two: is this caller allowed to touch this resource? Not allowed means reject — no ownership, no write.
Only after both gates pass do we enforce invariants — the rules that must always hold, like one order per cart.
Now the input is a valid, owned resource, so the write to Postgres is safe. Skip modeling and that double-click race writes twice.

resource-modeling.text: The senior tell is that the server owns identity and ownership, never the client. ownerId, id, status transitions, and timestamps are set server-side from the authenticated session — never read from the request body. The moment a field that decides 'who owns this' or 'what may this become' comes from untrusted input, you have an IDOR or a broken-object-authorization bug (OWASP API1/API3) waiting for the request you didn't imagine.

resource-modeling.title: Validate an order resource contract and its sum invariant
resource-modeling.summary: Implement a request contract validator that whitelists allowed fields, enforces types, and asserts the order invariant (line items sum equals total), then run it in the browser against fixed inputs.
resource-modeling.starter:
# Resource modeling lab: request contract + invariant.
#
# The lesson (in TypeScript/Zod) taught two ideas:
#   1. A STRICT request contract — the ONLY shape the outside world may send.
#      Unknown/extra fields (e.g. "isAdmin") must be REJECTED, not silently ignored.
#   2. An INVARIANT the resource must satisfy before it persists:
#      the client-asserted total must equal sum(qty * unitPrice) over items.
#
# Money is in integer cents. Ports this validation to plain Python.
#
# Fixed inputs (do not change these):
REQUESTS = [
    # 0: valid — sum = 2*500 + 1*250 = 1250
    {"cartId": "c1", "items": [{"sku": "A", "qty": 2, "unitPrice": 500},
                               {"sku": "B", "qty": 1, "unitPrice": 250}], "total": 1250},
    # 1: unknown field "isAdmin" must be rejected (strict whitelist)
    {"cartId": "c2", "items": [{"sku": "A", "qty": 1, "unitPrice": 100}],
     "total": 100, "isAdmin": True},
    # 2: invariant broken — declared total 999 != actual 900
    {"cartId": "c3", "items": [{"sku": "A", "qty": 3, "unitPrice": 300}], "total": 999},
    # 3: empty items list — contract requires at least one item
    {"cartId": "c4", "items": [], "total": 0},
    # 4: valid — sum = 4*125 = 500
    {"cartId": "c5", "items": [{"sku": "Z", "qty": 4, "unitPrice": 125}], "total": 500},
]

ALLOWED_TOP = {"cartId", "items", "total"}
ALLOWED_ITEM = {"sku", "qty", "unitPrice"}


class ContractError(Exception):
    pass


def validate(req):
    """Return the validated request dict, or raise ContractError with a reason.

    Rules (mirror the strict Zod contract + invariant):
      - Reject any top-level key not in ALLOWED_TOP -> "unknown field"
      - "items" must be a non-empty list                -> "empty items"
      - Reject any item key not in ALLOWED_ITEM          -> "unknown field"
      - total must equal sum(qty * unitPrice) over items -> "invariant"
    """
    # TODO: implement the checks above, raising ContractError(<reason>) on failure.
    raise NotImplementedError


for i, req in enumerate(REQUESTS):
    try:
        validate(req)
        print(f"{i}: OK")
    except ContractError as e:
        print(f"{i}: REJECT {e}")

2: REJECT invariant

4: OK

resource-modeling.intro: Prove your resource model holds — under bad input, not good:
items: Contract test: send a request with an extra field the schema doesn't list. It must be rejected (422), not silently dropped or persisted — that proves the strict schema (z.strictObject) closed mass-assignment.
Integrity test: send items whose quantities×prices do not equal total. The invariant must reject it before any write reaches the store.
Authorization test: as caller B, attempt to create a resource owned by caller A. It must return 403, and no row may be written — proves the auth boundary, not just the schema.

Idempotency replay: send the same create request twice with the same idempotency key. The second must return the first order, not create a duplicate — proves the exactly-once invariant the mission's double-click broke.
Response audit: confirm the response is a typed projection (OrderResponse), exposing no internal columns and no other caller's data — the outbound contract is enforced too.

api-contracts-schemas.outcome: Take one state-changing endpoint and write its API contract as an enforced schema: the request shape, the response shape, the validation that rejects bad input at the boundary, and the exact error envelope a caller gets back. Then prove the contract rejects what it should and an idempotency replay does not double-apply.
api-contracts-schemas.proof: Section 1 of api_contract_and_failure_repair_packet.md: a named request/response schema (Zod or equivalent), a contract test that PASSES on valid input and FAILS-with-422 on malformed input, and an idempotency-replay test showing the same key applied twice yields one state change. A reviewer reads the schema and can call your endpoint correctly without reading the handler.
api-contracts-schemas.unlock: Your contract is a schema validated at the boundary — not prose — and a test proves it rejects a malformed request with a typed error, not a 500.
api-contracts-schemas.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have an API contract if validation lives inside business logic three calls deep. A contract that is only enforced after the handler has already touched the database is not a boundary — it is a hope. The schema must reject at the door, before any side effect.

api-contracts-schemas.text: A partner integration goes live, and within an hour the orders table fills with rows where quantity is the string "two" and currency is null — because the endpoint trusted whatever JSON arrived. The contract was a paragraph in a wiki, not a schema at the door, so every bad request became a corrupted row instead of a clean 422.

An API contract is the promise a service makes about what it accepts and what it returns; the schema is that promise made executable, checked on every request. It sits at the foundation of Backend Engineering because every later concern — authorization, persistence, queues, observability, and not breaking callers on the next deploy — assumes the request was already validated and the response shape is stable.

api-contracts-schemas.prompt: Your handler starts with `const { amount, currency } = req.body` and goes straight to charging the card. A request arrives with amount as the string "100" and no currency. What actually happens, and where? Answer before reading on.
api-contracts-schemas.reveal: It does not fail at the door — it fails deep, as garbage. "100" * 1 coerces to 100 in some paths and NaN in others; missing currency becomes undefined, which your payment client may serialize as the literal "undefined" or default to USD. The bad request became a real charge in the wrong shape, discovered later in a reconciliation report. A schema at the boundary turns all of that into one deterministic 422 BEFORE any side effect — the request never reaches the card. Validation that lives in the handler validates too late to matter.

api-contracts-schemas.intro: Writing the contract, one line at a time. Trace one complete boundary decision before changing the handler.
steps: The request contract: amountCents is a positive integer — not a string, not a float of dollars. currency is a closed enum, so "usd" or null is rejected by the schema, not by a downstream surprise. This object IS the promise to callers.
The response contract: The output shape is named too. Parsing the response on the way out means you cannot accidentally leak an internal field or change the shape and break callers silently.

Parse at the boundary, FIRST: safeParse runs before any database call or side effect. On failure you return a typed 422 envelope with per-field errors — never a 500, never a half-applied write. This is the gate the whole lesson is about.

Idempotency check: Look up the request's idempotency key before doing work. If this exact request was already applied, return the stored result. This is what makes a retry safe — the network can replay, the charge cannot double.

Apply exactly once, in a transaction: Only validated, not-yet-seen requests reach the write — and the write is wrapped in a transaction so a mid-flight crash rolls back cleanly rather than leaving a partial charge. Validated data, one effect, atomic.

storyboard.say: A client fires a POST /payments request into the API gateway, which hands the raw JSON body straight to the front door.
The schema gate stands guard first: it parses every request against the declared contract before any side effect can run.
Bad shape fails fast. Quantity of 'two' or a null currency never reaches a handler; the gate returns a typed 422 envelope, not a 500.
That 422 goes back to the client with a repair path: fix the shape, then retry. The failure is legible, not a corrupted row.
Only validated requests pass to the idempotency check, which asks: is this a brand new key, or one we've already processed?
A replayed key short-circuits: it returns the stored result via the response schema, so a retry never double-charges the customer.
A new key reaches the handler, which writes to Postgres in a transaction, then maps the result into the response schema.
The response schema returns a 200 typed body. The contract guards both edges: no handler runs on unvalidated data, no untyped shape escapes.

api-contracts-schemas.text: The senior tell is the error envelope, not the happy path. Anyone can return 200 on good input; a contract you can trust returns a typed, machine-readable 422 with per-field errors on bad input — every time, in the same shape. This is the kind of gap OWASP API Security calls out: unvalidated input and verbose error responses (e.g., leaked 500 stack traces) fall under API8:2023 Security Misconfiguration — a top-10 API risk, not a style nit. (OWASP does not use the exact phrase 'leaked 500 stack traces'; leaking stack traces is an instance of Security Misconfiguration, and there is no standalone 'unvalidated input' item in the 2023 list.)

api-contracts-schemas.explanation: A real contract is proven by what it REJECTS and how it behaves under replay, not by a single happy path. Option 2 shows the boundary rejecting bad input as a typed 422 (not a leaked 500) and the idempotency key preventing a double-apply on retry — the two failure-path proofs the reviewer challenge demands. The happy-path test (1), prose docs (3), and one manual 200 (4) never exercise the failure path the contract exists to govern.

def _is_uuid(s: Any) -> bool:
    # Provided helper: True only for a lowercase-hex 8-4-4-4-12 UUID string.
    if not isinstance(s, str):

    for part, n in zip(parts, [8, 4, 4, 4, 12]):

validation-error-model.outcome: Design the Validation Error Model for one state-changing endpoint: a single structured error contract (status code + machine-readable body with per-field detail) that every rejection on that path obeys — wrong shape, failed auth, conflicting state, and a replayed request all answered the same way.
validation-error-model.proof: api_contract_and_failure_repair_packet.md with the error envelope schema, the status-code map (400 vs 401/403 vs 409 vs 422), one worked field-level rejection, and proof it holds: a contract test asserting the body shape plus an idempotency-replay returning the SAME error, not a second mutation. A peer hits the endpoint with bad input and parses the error programmatically without reading your code.
validation-error-model.unlock: Your error model gives one stable, parseable shape across every rejection class on the path, maps each class to the correct status code, and survives a replayed request without double-applying.
validation-error-model.doNotClaim: Do not claim a 'validation error model' if your endpoint returns a bare 500 with a stringified stack trace, or a 200 with {"ok": false} in the body. A leaked stack trace is an information-disclosure bug, and a 200-on-failure breaks every client that trusts the status line. A model is a contract clients can code against, not a place to dump whatever the exception said.

validation-error-model.text: A partner's checkout integration silently drops 8% of orders for a month. The cause: your endpoint answered invalid carts with HTTP 200 and a human sentence in the body, so their retry logic treated every rejection as success and never resubmitted. One ambiguous error model, thousands of lost orders, and not a single alert fired.

Every endpoint that changes state will be hit with input it must refuse — and a client on the other side has to tell 'you sent garbage, fix it' apart from 'try again later'. The Validation Error Model is the contract that makes refusal legible: it sits between your request/response contract and your persistence layer, and it is Section 2 of the proof packet you carry through this module.

validation-error-model.prompt: A POST /orders gets a negative quantity. You reject it. Which HTTP status — 400, 422, 500, or 200-with-an-error-flag? Decide before reading on.
validation-error-model.reveal: The instinct is 400, and 400 is defensible — but the sharper answer is 422 Unprocessable Content: the JSON parsed fine (so it is not a 400 malformed-syntax case), it was the meaning that failed validation. The real 'oh': the status code is not decoration, it is the first field of your error model. 500 says 'my fault, retry' and invites a retry storm against a request that will never succeed; 200 says 'success' and corrupts every client that trusts the status line. Picking the code IS designing the contract — clients branch on it before they ever read your body.

validation-error-model.intro: The contract, then the handler that obeys it. Trace one complete boundary decision before changing the handler.
steps: Declare the shape ONCE: Every rejection on this path returns a ProblemDetails. type is a stable URI clients can switch on; title is human but is NEVER the exception message — that is the information-disclosure leak the do-not-claim warns about.

The validation gate is a schema, not scattered ifs: One Zod object is the source of truth. Hand-rolled ifs drift: the schema cannot disagree with itself, and it generates the field-level errors for free.

Semantic failure → 422 + per-field errors[]: Map each Zod issue to {field, code, message}. The client highlights the exact bad field without parsing English. 422 (not 400) because the JSON parsed — it was the meaning that failed.

Idempotency BEFORE the write: This is the premium scenario's spine: a replayed Idempotency-Key returns the first stored response, so a retry never creates a second order. Exactly-once survives a flaky network.

Conflicts are 409, unknowns stay structured: A stock conflict is a CLIENT-meaningful 409, not a 500 — the difference between 'change your request' and 'retry later'. Even the re-thrown unknown must serialize as ProblemDetails, never a raw trace.

validation-error-model.text: A validation error model is a single response contract every rejection obeys: a correct status code (the class of failure), a stable parseable body, and field-level detail naming what failed and why. The invariant: the SHAPE never changes — only the contents. Clients code against the shape, not the prose.

validation-error-model.subtitle: POST /orders flows through four gates — parse, authorize, validate, persist. Each gate can REJECT, and every rejection exits through the one shared error model (status + structured body). The mutation only commits past all four.

storyboard.say: A client fires POST /orders. This request changes state, so it will be refused the moment its input is wrong.
Four gates stand between the request and the database: parse, authorize, validate, and idempotency, then finally the transaction.
Parse checks shape. Malformed JSON never reaches your logic; it exits as a 400 through the shared error model.
The auth boundary refuses unauthenticated or unauthorized callers, leaving as 401 or 403 through that same error model.
Semantic validation is where the silent-200 bug lived: an invalid cart must exit 422 with field detail, not a human sentence.
Idempotency and the transaction guard the write: a replay returns the same result, a conflict returns 409, both via the error model.
Only clearing all four gates commits the mutation and answers 201 Created.
Every rejection funnels into one parseable shape, so the client can always tell 'you sent garbage' from 'try again later'.

validation-error-model.text: Grounding, not vibes: OWASP API Security Top 10 lists Broken Object Level Authorization (API1) and Broken Object Property Level Authorization (API3, which absorbed the former 'Excessive Data Exposure') among the top risks; separately, a leaked stack trace in an error body is an instance of API8 Security Misconfiguration. (In the 2023 edition 'Excessive Data Exposure' is no longer its own entry, and a leaked stack trace maps to Security Misconfiguration, not to object/property authorization — so it does not 'hit both' of those authorization risks.) RFC 9457 (Problem Details) exists precisely so you do not invent a bespoke error shape per service. A sound design principle is that the contract is part of the design, not an afterthought (consistent with SWEBOK V4's Software Design knowledge area). The senior tell: their error model is designed with the success path, never bolted on after the demo.

validation-error-model.question: A reviewer says: 'Show me the exact evidence this isn't just a happy-path answer.' Which response actually proves the validation error model holds?
options: A screenshot of the endpoint returning 201 for a valid order.
A contract test asserting the 422 body shape for bad input, PLUS an idempotency-replay test proving a repeated request returns the same response and does not create a second row.
A paragraph in the README describing the intended error format.
A 500 handler that catches everything and logs it server-side.
validation-error-model.explanation: Proof of an error model is proof of the REJECTION paths, not the success path. The contract test pins the structured body so clients can rely on the shape; the idempotency-replay test pins the exactly-once invariant the premium scenario demands. The 201 screenshot (1) only shows the happy path; a README (3) is intent, not evidence; a catch-all 500 (4) is the failure mode — it erases the very distinctions the model exists to make.

          field_error("quantity", "not_positive", "quantity must be a positive integer")

        {"type": PROBLEM_TYPE, "title": PROBLEM_TITLE, "status": 422, "errors": [...]}
    (check "sku" before "quantity" so the errors[] order is stable).

    Otherwise return the success dict:
        {"status": 201, "sku": <sku>, "quantity": <quantity>}

    {"sku": "WIDGET-1", "quantity": 3},
    {"sku": "", "quantity": 0},
    {"sku": "BOLT-9", "quantity": -2},

A billing endpoint maps a declined card to a structured 402 with a decline-code field, never a 500 the client retries into a double-charge. A webhook receiver returns a stable error body so the sender's retry-with-backoff can tell 'malformed payload, give up' from 'I'm down, resend'. A queue worker writes the same field-level rejection to a dead-letter record so an operator can triage without reading code. What stays invariant: one shape, the right status class, machine-readable detail, exactly-once under replay. What changes is the status vocabulary (402 vs 409 vs a DLQ reason) and who reads it — a partner, a sender, or an on-call operator. Carry api_contract_and_failure_repair_packet.md into the capstone: it is not 'I understand validation errors,' it is 'here is an endpoint I made refuse correctly, and here is the test that proves it.'

http-status-codes.outcome: Take one state-changing endpoint (POST /payments, or a realistic one) and write its status-code contract: which code each path returns — success, validation failure, auth failure, conflict, server fault — and what the client is supposed to DO on each. Then prove the codes match the behavior, including a duplicate request that must return the same answer twice.
http-status-codes.proof: The `Status Codes` section of api_contract_and_failure_repair_packet.md: a path-by-code table where every code carries a client action, plus a replay test showing a retried POST returns 200/201 the second time (not a second charge). A reviewer reads the table and can predict the response of any request without running it.
http-status-codes.unlock: Your contract maps each path to a status class that tells the client whether to retry, fix-and-resend, re-auth, or stop — and an idempotent replay returns a safe, identical result.
http-status-codes.doNotClaim: Do not claim a status-code contract if every error is a 500 or every error is a 200 with `{"error": ...}` in the body. A code the client cannot branch on is decoration. The status code IS the contract; the body is the detail.

http-status-codes.text: A customer's card gets charged twice. The retry on a flaky network hit your endpoint a second time, your handler returned 500 the first time after the charge succeeded, and the client — seeing 500 — retried. Nobody decided what 500 meant. The status code was the contract, and it lied.

This sits in the foundation phase of Backend Engineering: it turns the HTTP contract from earlier request/response lessons into a precise, machine-readable promise. The status code is the one byte every client, proxy, retry library, and load balancer reads BEFORE the body — get it wrong and correct code downstream does the wrong thing.

http-status-codes.prompt: A POST that creates a payment fails because the amount is negative. Your handler returns `200 OK` with `{"error": "invalid amount"}`. What breaks downstream — even though your message is perfectly clear? Answer before reading on.
http-status-codes.reveal: Everything that reads the code instead of your body. The client's HTTP library sees 200 and resolves the promise as success; the retry middleware never fires; the dashboard graphs it as a healthy request; the proxy may cache it. Your message is human-readable and machine-invisible. 200-with-an-error-body is the most common way a status-code contract silently fails: the one field every layer agrees to read says 'fine' while the truth is in a field only your frontend parses.

http-status-codes.intro: The handler that makes the contract true. Trace one complete boundary decision before changing the handler.
steps: Declare the success code up front: 201 Created — not 200 — because a POST that creates a resource should announce the creation. The default code is part of the contract, not an afterthought.

Client error → 422, never 200: The body is bad, so the CLIENT must fix and resend. A 4xx tells their retry library 'do not blind-retry this — it will fail identically.' Returning 200 here is the pretest trap.
Auth boundary → 403: Distinct from 401 (not authenticated) — 403 means authenticated but forbidden. Conflating them costs the client the ability to decide between re-login and stop.
Idempotency replay → identical result: A retry with the same Idempotency-Key returns the STORED response, same status, no second charge. This is the line that fixes the double-charge in the mission.
Conflict → 409: A duplicate or stale-state collision is the client's to reconcile, not a server fault. 409 says 'your request conflicts with current state', not 'we broke'.
Infra fault → 503, safe to retry: 5xx is the one class that INVITES retry. 503 (provider down) tells the client to back off and try again — the opposite signal from the 4xx above.
http-status-codes.commonMistake: One code for five futures — the client is blind

http-status-codes.title: The status code is a contract about what the CLIENT does next
http-status-codes.text: 2xx: succeeded, stop. 4xx: YOU sent a bad request — fix it, don't blind-retry. 401/403: re-authenticate or you're forbidden. 409: it conflicts with current state. 5xx: WE failed — safe to retry. The invariant: the code must match the action the client should take.

http-status-codes.subtitle: A POST /payments handler is a decision tree, and each leaf is a status code that tells the client what to do next. The failure path (charge succeeds, handler 500s) and the repair (idempotency key replays the stored result) are both on the map.

storyboard.say: One POST /payments enters the handler. Everything after this is a decision tree, and each leaf is a status code that tells the client what to do next.
First gate: is the body well-formed? If not, we return 422 Unprocessable — a 4xx that says you sent bad input, so fix it, don't blind-retry.
Valid body reaches the auth boundary. No credentials or forbidden gets 401 or 403 — re-authenticate; a retry with the same token won't help.
Allowed requests hit the idempotency store. If the key was seen before, we replay the stored result as 201 — the retry-safety net that stops double charges.
A new key proceeds to charge and persist. On a conflict with current state — a duplicate or stale write — we answer 409, not a blind success.
Clean commit returns 201 Created — succeeded, stop. This is the one 2xx leaf the whole tree is trying to reach honestly.
But if the DB dies after the charge, we return 500 — WE failed, safe to retry. The idempotency key makes that retry replay 201 instead of charging twice.
The invariant: the status code is the contract. It must match the action the client should take — get it wrong and correct downstream code does the wrong thing.

http-status-codes.caption: OWASP API Security (API8 Security Misconfiguration) flags leaking detail in error bodies; hiding real failures behind 200 responses is a sound engineering concern but is not something the OWASP API Top 10 explicitly names. The status class is the safe, machine-readable channel; the body is where you stay sparing.

http-status-codes.text: The senior tell: the dangerous failures are not the loud 500s — they're the 200s that hide an error and the 5xx that leaks a stack trace. (Only the stack-trace-leak half maps to OWASP API Top 10 via API8 Security Misconfiguration; the '200 that hides an error' pattern is not named in the OWASP API Top 10, so the blanket 'grounded in OWASP API Top 10' framing overstates the authority.) Pick the code by what the CLIENT must do (retry / fix / re-auth / reconcile / stop), then keep the body minimal. A correct status code with a vague body beats a 200 with a perfect error message every time, because every layer between you and the user reads the code and almost none read the body.

http-status-codes.question: Reviewer challenge: a teammate's POST /orders returns 500 when the request body is missing a required field. Why is that the wrong code, and what is the cost in production?
options: It is fine — any error can be a 500, the body explains the rest.

A missing field is a CLIENT error (4xx, e.g. 422/400), not a server fault (5xx). Returning 500 tells retry libraries to re-send the identical bad request, inflates your error-rate SLO with non-incidents, and pages on-call for a problem only the caller can fix.
It should be a 200 so the client's promise resolves cleanly.
It should be a 404 because the order was not created.
http-status-codes.explanation: 5xx means WE failed and a retry might work; 4xx means YOU sent something we can't process and retrying unchanged won't help. A malformed body is squarely 4xx. Mislabeling it 5xx triggers automatic retries of a doomed request, corrupts your reliability metrics and error budgets, and wakes on-call for a caller bug — the exact 'happy-path answer' the reviewer is hunting for. (DORA's change-fail rate measures deployments that fail, not per-request 5xx rates; conflating an HTTP status mislabel with DORA change-failure-rate misuses the metric — drop the DORA parenthetical or replace with 'SLO/error budgets'.)

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Result:
    status: int
    body: str


class DuplicateChargeError(Exception):
    """Raised when this order was already charged."""


class InfraError(Exception):
    """Raised when the payment provider is unreachable."""


# Idempotency store: an idem_key already seen means we REPLAY the stored
# result instead of charging again.
_IDEM_STORE = {
    "idem-existing": Result(201, "charged:acct-7:1500"),
}


def charge_and_persist(account_id, amount, idem_key, infra_ok, duplicate):
    """Simulated charge. Do not modify."""
    if not infra_ok:
        raise InfraError()
    if duplicate:
        raise DuplicateChargeError()
    return Result(201, f"charged:{account_id}:{amount}")

    """
    Return a Result(status, body) using the correct HTTP status code.

    Apply the checks IN THIS ORDER (first match wins):

      2. not can_charge            -> 403, "not allowed to charge this account"
      3. idem_key already in store -> replay the stored Result (no re-charge)
      4. call charge_and_persist(...); on success return its Result
           - DuplicateChargeError  -> 409, "payment already exists for this order"
           - InfraError            -> 503, "payment provider unavailable"

    TODO: implement the ladder above and return the right Result.

REQUESTS = [
    ("R1", dict(amount=1500, account_id="acct-7", idem_key="idem-new-1", can_charge=True,  infra_ok=True,  duplicate=False)),
    ("R2", dict(amount=0,    account_id="acct-7", idem_key="idem-new-2", can_charge=True,  infra_ok=True,  duplicate=False)),
    ("R3", dict(amount=200,  account_id="acct-9", idem_key="idem-new-3", can_charge=False, infra_ok=True,  duplicate=False)),
    ("R4", dict(amount=1500, account_id="acct-7", idem_key="idem-existing", can_charge=True, infra_ok=True, duplicate=False)),
    ("R5", dict(amount=800,  account_id="acct-7", idem_key="idem-new-5", can_charge=True,  infra_ok=True,  duplicate=True)),

pagination-filtering-sorting.outcome: Take one real list endpoint (GET /orders or similar) and make it production-shaped: cursor (keyset) pagination with a bounded page size, an allowlisted filter + sort contract, and a query that cannot be injected or knocked over by a deep page. Capture it as api_contract_and_failure_repair_packet.md.
pagination-filtering-sorting.proof: api_contract_and_failure_repair_packet.md with: the request/response contract (filter params, sort allowlist, limit cap, next_cursor), the rejected approach (OFFSET pagination) and why, the expected failure you broke (drift or injection), the verification method (a contract test + a deep-page query plan), one reviewer objection, and the capstone reuse note. A reviewer can page from first to last with zero dupes and zero gaps.
pagination-filtering-sorting.unlock: Your endpoint pages by keyset (not OFFSET), caps the limit, allowlists sort columns + direction, and returns an opaque next_cursor — proven by a test that pages to the end with no duplicates.
pagination-filtering-sorting.doNotClaim: Do not claim 'pagination works' from a screenshot of page 1. Page 1 always looks fine. The skill lives at the seam between pages and at page 5,000 — if you have not paged to the end while rows are being inserted, you have not tested pagination, you have tested a SELECT with a LIMIT.

pagination-filtering-sorting.text: A customer exports their order history, scrolls to page 2, and sees three orders that were already on page 1 — and never sees the four that fell through the crack. Nobody wrote a bug. Someone wrote OFFSET 20 over a table that keeps getting new rows.

Every list endpoint that ships unbounded is a latent outage: one client asks for all 4M rows, sorts by an un-indexed column, and takes the database down. Pagination, filtering, and sorting are one contract — the invariant is a stable, bounded, injection-proof window over a moving result set.

pagination-filtering-sorting.prompt: Your endpoint does ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40 to fetch page 3. Rows are being inserted at the top while users page. What goes wrong — and why does page 1 still look perfect in the demo?
pagination-filtering-sorting.reveal: OFFSET counts rows from the current result set, not from where the user was. Insert two rows at the top and OFFSET 40 now points two rows earlier than last time — the user re-sees rows (duplicates) and skips rows (gaps). The demo passes because in a quiet demo nothing is being inserted between page loads. The bug is invisible until there is concurrent write traffic — i.e. always, in production. Keyset pagination fixes it by remembering WHERE you were (the last row's key), not HOW FAR you scrolled.

pagination-filtering-sorting.intro: The gold handler — keyset, capped, allowlisted. Trace one complete boundary decision before changing the handler.
steps: Allowlist + cap as constants: SORTABLE maps a public sort name to a real column; an unknown sort falls back, never reaches SQL. MAX_LIMIT is the ceiling that stops 'give me 4 million rows'.
Bound the limit: Math.min caps it and the || 20 handles garbage input. This single line is the difference between a slow endpoint and a database outage.

Resolve sort through the allowlist: q.get('sort') is a user string. It is used only as a KEY into SORTABLE — the value put into SQL is a column you control. This is how ORDER BY stops being an injection vector.
Decode the opaque cursor: The cursor carries the last row's (sort key, id) — its position, not its page number. Opaque so clients cannot forge offsets or leak internals.

The keyset WHERE — the whole trick: (sort_key, id) < (cursor.key, cursor.id) on a composite index seeks straight to where you left off. id is the tiebreaker that makes the order total, so no row is ever duplicated or skipped under concurrent inserts.
LIMIT n+1 → hasMore: Fetch one extra row. If it comes back, there is a next page; you slice it off and mint next_cursor from the genuine last item. No second COUNT(*) query, no OFFSET.

storyboard.say: A customer exports order history and hits GET /orders. The client's raw query string is where every control begins.
The API handler hands the raw params straight to the contract check. It trusts nothing it received yet.
Validation is the choke point: it allowlists which columns you may sort and filter, caps the limit, and forbids any user string reaching SQL.
Skip that check and you take the warning branch: OFFSET drift, an unbounded scan, or an injected ORDER BY that can down the database.
Pass it, and only safe, bounded input reaches the keyset query that pages by the last row's sort key, never by OFFSET.
The keyset WHERE seeks straight into the composite index on (sort_key, id) — a targeted seek, not a full-table scan.
It fetches limit plus one row: the extra row becomes hasMore and yields an opaque next_cursor in the response.
The invariant holds: stable order under concurrent writes, a hard ceiling on work, and no page-2 row ever repeating page 1.

pagination-filtering-sorting.text: OWASP API4 (Unrestricted Resource Consumption) names the uncapped limit explicitly: a list endpoint with no maximum page size is a denial-of-service primitive, not a convenience. And the tell of a senior backend engineer is the tiebreaker — they always sort by (business_key, id), never business_key alone, because a non-unique sort column makes the page boundary ambiguous and silently reintroduces the duplicate/gap bug keyset was supposed to kill.

pagination-filtering-sorting.question: A reviewer says: 'Show me the exact evidence this is not just a happy-path answer.' Which single piece of evidence best proves the pagination contract holds?
options: A screenshot of page 1 rendering 20 orders correctly.

A test that pages from the first cursor to next_cursor === null while rows are inserted, asserting every id appears exactly once (no dupes, no gaps), plus an EXPLAIN showing an index seek at a deep cursor.
A comment in the code saying '// keyset pagination, no OFFSET'.
A load test showing the endpoint returns 200 OK under traffic.
pagination-filtering-sorting.explanation: The invariant is 'each row appears exactly once across the full traversal, under concurrent writes.' Only option 2 proves it — it walks the whole result set via cursors (not page numbers) while inserts happen, asserts the no-dupe/no-gap property, and the EXPLAIN proves deep pages stay O(limit) instead of scanning. Page-1 screenshots (1), comments (3), and a 200 status (4) are exactly the happy-path theater the reviewer is asking you to get past.

idempotency-retry-safety.outcome: Take one real state-changing endpoint (a payment charge, an order create, a webhook handler) and make it safe to retry: add an idempotency key, persist it inside the same database transaction as the effect, and return the first response on every replay. Capture it in api_contract_and_failure_repair_packet.md.
idempotency-retry-safety.proof: api_contract_and_failure_repair_packet.md with: the HTTP contract (Idempotency-Key header), the selected approach, the rejected approach, the expected failure, the verification method (replay the same key, assert one charge), a reviewer objection, and the capstone connection. A replay test fires the same key twice and proves exactly one side effect.
idempotency-retry-safety.unlock: A duplicate request with the same idempotency key produces exactly one effect and returns the original response — proven by a replay test, not by claim.
idempotency-retry-safety.doNotClaim: Do not claim idempotency because the request 'looks the same'. Identical payloads are not the invariant — a stored, transaction-bound idempotency key is. If the dedupe check and the write are not in one atomic unit, you have a race, not safety.

idempotency-retry-safety.text: The customer's card was charged three times. The app didn't double-submit — the network timed out, the mobile client retried twice, and your 'charge' handler ran clean each time because nothing told it this was the same request.

Retries are not an edge case; they are the default in any distributed system — clients, gateways, and queue workers all retry on timeout. Idempotency retry safety is the contract that lets a request arrive twice and change the world once, which is Section 1 of the packet you carry into the capstone.

idempotency-retry-safety.prompt: Your POST /charges returns 200, but the client never got the response — the connection dropped. The client retries the exact same request. What does a naive handler do, and why is 'just check if a charge already exists' not enough? Answer before reading on.
idempotency-retry-safety.reveal: The naive handler charges again — the second request is indistinguishable from a real new charge. And 'check if one exists first' is a race: two retries can both pass the check before either writes, so both charge. The fix is not a lookup before the write; it is a unique idempotency key reserved in the SAME transaction as the effect, so the database — not your code's timing — enforces exactly-once.

idempotency-retry-safety.intro: Making POST /charges replay-safe, line by line. Trace one complete boundary decision before changing the handler.
steps: The HTTP contract: The Idempotency-Key header is the request's identity. No key, no safety — reject at the boundary rather than guess.
One transaction wraps everything: The dedupe read, the effect write, and the key insert all commit together or roll back together. This is the whole invariant.
Replay short-circuit: If the key already has a stored result, return it untouched. This is what makes the second, third, Nth request safe.
The effect: Write the charge and build the response. Not yet visible to anyone — the transaction hasn't committed.

The UNIQUE constraint is the enforcer: Two retries can both pass find() at line 7. Only one survives the insert here; the loser's transaction rolls back and retries into the replay branch. The database, not your timing, guarantees exactly-once.

Pass the key downstream too: Stripe and most gateways accept their own idempotency key. Forward it so even a partial-commit retry can't double-charge externally. But the DB transaction cannot roll back an external charge: if the gateway succeeds and the COMMIT then fails, you have a charge with no record. It is the gateway's OWN idempotency key (not the DB transaction) that makes the external effect exactly-once — and holding DB row locks across a network call is itself a cost. A transactional outbox avoids this.

idempotency-retry-safety.title: One key, one effect — enforced by the transaction, not by a pre-check
idempotency-retry-safety.text: The client sends an Idempotency-Key. The server stores that key with the result inside the same DB transaction as the side effect. A unique constraint makes the second insert fail, so a replay returns the first response. The invariant: dedupe and effect commit atomically, or not at all.

The handler reserves the key and writes the charge in ONE transaction; the unique constraint on the keys store is what enforces exactly-once. A replay hits the stored result and skips the gateway entirely. The failure path is the dashed retry; the repair is the keys store.

storyboard.say: A client sends the charge request, attaching an Idempotency-Key so the server can recognize this exact request if it ever arrives again.
The handler opens one transaction and reserves the key in the idempotency store — a unique constraint here is what will enforce exactly-once.
Inside that same transaction, it writes the charge to the charges table — dedupe and effect commit together, or not at all.
Only after the key is reserved does the handler hit the payment gateway to charge the card exactly once.
Now the timeout: the mobile client retries. The replay arrives, but the key already exists in the store.
The store returns the first stored result — the gateway is skipped entirely, so the card is never charged a second time.
The invariant: a request can arrive twice and change the world exactly once — the unique constraint on the keys store is the repair.

idempotency-retry-safety.caption: The difference is not 'do you check' — both check. It's whether the database enforces uniqueness atomically with the effect, or your code hopes the timing works out.

idempotency-retry-safety.text: Retry-safety is both a correctness property (no duplicate effects) and a security property — a duplicate-submission bug is also an abuse vector (replayed payments, doubled credits). Replayed state-changing requests relate to OWASP API6:2023 (Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows), where idempotency keys are a commonly recommended MITIGATION — the Top 10 text itself doesn't name retry-safety. The senior tell — scope the key's lifetime and store the response, not just the key. A key with no stored result can't answer a replay; a key that never expires leaks storage forever. Bound it (24h is a common TTL) and store the exact body you returned.

idempotency-retry-safety.question: Reviewer challenge: a teammate says 'my handler is idempotent because it checks for an existing charge before inserting.' What is the exact evidence that proves this is NOT safe under retries?
options: Show that the payloads of the two requests are byte-identical.
Run two concurrent requests with the same idempotency key against the real DB and show two charges committed because the check and the insert are not in one transaction.
Confirm the endpoint returns 200 on the happy path.
Point out that the handler has no logging.
idempotency-retry-safety.explanation: Idempotency is an atomicity property, so the proof is a concurrency test, not a payload comparison. Two parallel retries can both pass a separate pre-check before either commits — the only thing that prevents the double-write is a unique constraint enforced inside the same transaction as the effect. Identical payloads (option 1) and a green happy path (option 3) say nothing about the race.

idempotency-retry-safety.title: Make a charge processor idempotent by key
idempotency-retry-safety.summary: Implement create_charge so duplicate Idempotency-Keys replay the stored result instead of charging again, then run it in the browser.
idempotency-retry-safety.starter:
# ── Idempotency-Key charge processor ─────────────────────────────────
# Port the lesson's transactional idempotency pattern to Python.
#
# Rules (mirror the lesson's TS handler):
#   1. Every request carries an Idempotency-Key.
#   2. If the key was seen before, REPLAY the stored result. Do NOT charge
#      the gateway again, and do NOT allocate a new charge id.
#   3. If the key is new, allocate the next charge id, store {key: result},
#      then call the gateway exactly once.
#
# The UNIQUE(key) index guarantees a repeated key never creates a second
# charge; replays return the identical first response.


class ChargeProcessor:
    def __init__(self):
        self._store = {}          # key -> result (UNIQUE idempotency_keys table)
        self._next_id = 1         # charge id sequence
        self.gateway_calls = 0    # times the payment gateway was hit

    def create_charge(self, key, amount):
        # TODO:
        #   - if `key` is already in self._store, return the stored result
        #     (a replay: no new id, no gateway call).
        #   - otherwise: take the next id from self._next_id (then increment),
        #     build result = {"id": <id>, "status": "captured", "amount": amount},
        #     store it under `key`, increment self.gateway_calls by 1,
        #     and return result.
        raise NotImplementedError


# Fixed input: (idempotency_key, amount) in arrival order.
# k1, k2, and k3 each retry once — those retries must replay, not re-charge.
REQUESTS = [
    ("k1", 1000),
    ("k2", 2500),
    ("k1", 1000),   # retry of k1
    ("k3",  500),
    ("k3",  500),   # retry of k3
    ("k2", 2500),   # retry of k2
]

p = ChargeProcessor()
for key, amount in REQUESTS:
    r = p.create_charge(key, amount)
    print(f"{key} -> id={r['id']} status={r['status']} amount={r['amount']}")

print(f"gateway_calls={p.gateway_calls}")
print(f"unique_charges={p._next_id - 1}")

idempotency-retry-safety.intro: Prove the endpoint is retry-safe — no vibes:
items: Contract test: a request without an Idempotency-Key is rejected at the boundary (400), not silently processed.
Replay test: fire the same key twice sequentially → assert exactly one row in the effect table and one downstream gateway call.
Concurrency test: fire two requests with the same key in parallel → exactly one effect commits; the other returns the stored result, not an error.
Rollback evidence: force the effect write to fail mid-transaction → confirm the idempotency key was NOT persisted (no orphan key that would block a legitimate retry).
Replay returns the ORIGINAL response body, byte-for-byte — not a fresh 'already processed' message the client didn't expect.

prompts: In your own words: why is 'check if it already exists, then write' a race, and what specifically does putting the key insert inside the transaction fix?
Explain why payload equality is the wrong invariant for idempotency and a stored idempotency key is the right one — using your own endpoint as the example.
Walk through what happens on a replay step by step: where does the second request stop, and what does the client receive?

idempotency-retry-safety.excellent: Passing evidence plus an unseen failure, retained regression, operational tradeoff, and this transfer: The same key-in-transaction move travels across every state-changing boundary. A webhook handler dedupes on the provider's event ID so a redelivered Stripe event credits an account once. A queue worker stores the message ID before acking so an at-least-once redelivery doesn't re-run the job. An internal API that mutates inventory keys on a client request ID. auth-authorization-boundaries.outcome: Take one state-changing API endpoint and draw its auth boundary: prove that every request enforces authorization against the authenticated principal AND the specific object, not just a valid token. Capture it as a reviewable packet — the boundary, the failure you fear (BOLA/IDOR), the kill-test, and the repair.
auth-authorization-boundaries.proof: api_contract_and_failure_repair_packet.md with: the endpoint contract, the auth boundary (who is the principal, what object, what rule), the expected failure (object-level authorization bypass), a contract/integration test that returns 403 when a valid token requests another tenant's object, and the repair note. A reviewer can replay the cross-tenant request and watch it get denied.
auth-authorization-boundaries.unlock: Your packet names the principal, the object, the authorization rule enforced server-side, and a test where a fully-authenticated token is still denied the wrong object.
auth-authorization-boundaries.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have an auth boundary because the route is behind a login. Authentication answers 'who are you'; authorization answers 'may you touch THIS'. A 200 for a valid token on someone else's order is the exact failure this lesson exists to kill — being logged in is not permission.

auth-authorization-boundaries.text: GET /api/orders/1043 returns the order. A curious user edits the URL to /api/orders/1044 and reads a stranger's invoice — name, address, card last four. The token was valid the whole time; nobody ever checked that 1044 was theirs. That single missing line is OWASP API Top 10 #1, and it ships to production constantly.

This lesson sits in the applied-skill phase of Backend Engineering: you already write request/response contracts and validate input — now you make authorization a boundary the request cannot cross. The auth boundary is Section 1 of the api_contract_and_failure_repair_packet.md you carry through validation, persistence, and the capstone.

auth-authorization-boundaries.prompt: Your endpoint requires a valid JWT, and the request arrives with one. A logged-in user requests /api/orders/1044 — an order that belongs to a different customer. Is returning it a bug? Decide before reading.
auth-authorization-boundaries.reveal: Yes — and the most common high-severity one in production APIs. A valid token proves authentication (who you are), not authorization (what you may touch). Trusting the client-supplied object id `1044` without checking it belongs to the authenticated principal is Broken Object-Level Authorization (BOLA / IDOR). The boundary is not the login wall; it is the per-object ownership check on every single request, enforced server-side, every time.

auth-authorization-boundaries.intro: Closing the boundary in the handler, line by line. Trace one complete boundary decision before changing the handler.
steps: Principal from the token, never the body: The authn middleware sets req.principal from the verified JWT. If the handler reads customer_id from the request body or a query param, the client picks their own identity — instant privilege escalation.
Load the object first, 404 if absent: You cannot authorize against an object you have not loaded. Return 404 (not 403) for missing rows so you do not leak which ids exist.

The authorization boundary: order.customerId !== principal.customerId is the whole skill in one line: the authenticated principal compared to the specific object's owner. This runs on EVERY request — there is no cache, no skip.
Log the denial as a security signal: An authz_denied log line with principal + object id is your observability hook: a spike of these is an enumeration attack in progress.
403, not 404, on ownership failure: The object exists but you may not have it → 403 Forbidden. (Some teams return 404 to hide existence; either is defensible — picking deliberately is the judgment.)
Only now return the data: The DTO is emitted strictly after the boundary passes. No early return, no logging the body before the check — the boundary gates the response, not the other way around.

auth-authorization-boundaries.title: Authentication is the door; authorization is the boundary on every object
auth-authorization-boundaries.text: The invariant: every request re-derives the principal from the trusted token and checks that principal against the specific object before acting. Never trust a client-supplied id or role to grant access. Authenticated is not authorized.

auth-authorization-boundaries.title: Where the auth boundary lives in the request path
auth-authorization-boundaries.subtitle: Authn happens once at the gateway; authz must happen again at the handler, against the object the request names. The dashed edge is the failure: skipping the ownership check.

legend.label: trusted principal flows from authn → handler
the authz boundary — enforced per object, every request
the failure path: object check skipped (BOLA)

storyboard.say: A request enters: the client sends its Bearer token plus the object id it wants, here order 1043.
The gateway authenticates once, verifying the token and passing a trusted principal down to the handler.
The handler loads the object the request named from Postgres, using the client-supplied id verbatim.
Now the real question: does this authenticated principal actually own this specific object?
When ownership fails, the check denies the request with a 403 — the principal is authenticated but not authorized.
The dashed edge is the bug: skip the check and a valid token returns a stranger's data with a cheerful 200.
The invariant: re-derive the principal from the trusted token and check it against the object every time. Authenticated is not authorized.

auth-authorization-boundaries.caption: The weak version is indistinguishable from secure on the happy path — your own data always returns 200. The breach only appears when someone else's id is requested, which is exactly the test the weak version never wrote.

auth-authorization-boundaries.text: OWASP grounds this: Broken Object-Level Authorization is API Security Top 10 #1. OWASP attributes its severity to the wide attack surface of endpoints that expose object identifiers with inadequate object-level access control; in practice the happy-path test still passes and the boundary is often one easy-to-omit line. The senior tell is testing authorization with a VALID token for the WRONG object — not an expired or missing one. Anyone tests the locked door; pros test whether a real key opens the wrong lock.

auth-authorization-boundaries.question: A reviewer says: 'Show me the exact evidence this endpoint isn't just happy-path-safe.' Which artifact actually proves the auth boundary holds?
options: A test that an expired or missing token returns 401.
A test where a fully valid token for customer A requests customer B's object and receives 403 — plus the server-side ownership check it exercises.
A comment in the handler saying '// auth required'.
Confirmation the route is registered behind the login middleware.
auth-authorization-boundaries.explanation: Only option 2 tests authorization rather than authentication. 401-on-bad-token (1) and login middleware (4) prove the door is locked — they say nothing about object-level access. The comment (3) is documentation, not enforcement. The boundary is only proven when a genuinely authenticated principal is denied an object it does not own; that 403 is the irreplaceable evidence.

auth-authorization-boundaries.title: Enforce object-level authorization on order lookups
auth-authorization-boundaries.summary: Implement get_order so it enforces the authz boundary — an authenticated principal may only read orders they own — then run it in the browser to see each request resolve to 200/401/403/404.
auth-authorization-boundaries.starter:
"""
Lesson: Authorization boundaries.

The dangerous bug is not "who are you?" (authentication) but
"do you own THIS specific object?" (object-level authorization).
A valid, logged-in customer must still be BLOCKED from reading
another customer's order.

Implement get_order(principal_customer_id, order_id) to return an
(status_code, body) tuple following this exact precedence:

  1. principal_customer_id is None      -> (401, "unauthenticated")
  2. order_id not in ORDERS             -> (404, "not_found")
  3. order is not owned by principal    -> (403, "forbidden")
  4. otherwise                          -> (200, {"id": ..., "total": ...})

Order matters: check auth first, then existence, then ownership.
On success, return ONLY the id and total (a DTO), not the raw row.
"""

# Fixed data (the "database"). Do not change.
ORDERS = {
    101: {"id": 101, "customer_id": "cust_A", "total": 4200},
    102: {"id": 102, "customer_id": "cust_B", "total": 1599},
    103: {"id": 103, "customer_id": "cust_A", "total": 900},
    104: {"id": 104, "customer_id": "cust_C", "total": 250},
}


def get_order(principal_customer_id, order_id):
    # TODO: implement the authorization boundary described above.
    # Return an (int_status_code, body) tuple.
    raise NotImplementedError


# Fixed request log (the "traffic"). Do not change.
REQUESTS = [
    (None, 101),        # not authenticated
    ("cust_A", 101),    # owner reads own order
    ("cust_A", 102),    # A tries to read B's order  -> denied
    ("cust_B", 102),    # owner reads own order
    ("cust_A", 999),    # order does not exist
    ("cust_C", 104),    # owner reads own order
    ("cust_A", 104),    # A tries to read C's order  -> denied
]

for principal, oid in REQUESTS:
    status, body = get_order(principal, oid)
    print(f"{principal}|{oid} -> {status} {body}")

An integration test sends a VALID token for one principal against another principal's object and asserts 403 (or 404-by-policy). If you only test 401 on bad tokens, you tested authentication, not authorization — add the cross-tenant case.

persistence-repository-boundary.outcome: Take one state-changing endpoint (or a realistic one) and put a Persistence Repository Boundary on it: the service talks to a repository interface, never to the ORM/SQL directly. Then write api_contract_and_failure_repair_packet.md proving the boundary holds under one realistic failure.

A reviewer can swap the storage implementation behind the interface without touching a line of service logic.
persistence-repository-boundary.unlock: Your service depends on a repository INTERFACE; persistence details (SQL, ORM, transaction handling) live behind it; and a replayed request neither double-writes nor leaves a partial write.
persistence-repository-boundary.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have a repository boundary if your service still imports the ORM, builds queries inline, or knows table names. Wrapping `db.query(...)` in a function called `repository` is not a boundary — it is a rename. The boundary is real only when the service cannot tell which database is underneath.

persistence-repository-boundary.text: The endpoint worked in every demo. Then a client retried a timed-out POST /charges, your handler re-ran the INSERT, and one customer got billed twice — because the service was wired straight into the database with no boundary to catch the replay.

A state-changing endpoint must persist exactly once, validate, authorize, and roll back cleanly under failure. The Persistence Repository Boundary is the seam that makes those guarantees the storage layer's job — not something smeared through your service code.

persistence-repository-boundary.prompt: Your order service calls `db.insert('orders', row)` directly inside the handler. Before we add anything — what is the real cost of that, beyond "it's a bit ugly"? Answer before reading on.
persistence-repository-boundary.reveal: It fuses three concerns the database should own — transaction control, idempotency, and rollback — into business code that can't enforce them. With no boundary, every caller re-implements "insert exactly once" by hand, so a retry double-writes, a mid-write crash leaves a half-saved order, and you cannot test the service without a live database. The boundary isn't tidiness; it's where exactly-once actually lives.

persistence-repository-boundary.intro: Building the boundary, one piece at a time. Trace one complete boundary decision before changing the handler.
steps: The boundary itself: A pure interface — no `Pool`, no SQL, no `orders` table name. This is the contract the service is written against; everything else is swappable behind it.
Service depends on the interface: `OrderService` takes an `OrderRepository`, never a database handle. You can hand it a Postgres impl in prod and a fake in tests — same service, zero changes.
Idempotency check, not a re-insert: On a replayed request the service returns the prior order. This is the exactly-once guarantee, expressed in business terms, not SQL.

The transaction lives behind the boundary: BEGIN → INSERT → COMMIT in one connection. The unique constraint on idempotency_key turns a concurrent double-submit into a caught error, not a double charge.
Rollback makes partial writes impossible: Any failure past BEGIN rolls back the whole unit. The service never wrote rollback logic — it can't, and shouldn't. That's the boundary earning its place.

storyboard.say: A client fires POST /orders, then its connection times out — so it retries. The same command arrives twice at your API handler.
The handler validates the request and hands a clean command to the Order Service — the last place raw input is checked.
Here's the seam: the service depends on the OrderRepository interface — just save and findById — and never touches SQL or the ORM directly.
This is the mistake that double-billed a customer: wiring the service straight to the database means the retry re-runs the INSERT.
The repository implementation owns the write — it opens one transaction and persists everything atomically, ready to roll back on failure.
It also owns the idempotency key: the retried command maps to the same key, so the second INSERT is caught and the charge happens exactly once.
The invariant: the ORM lives only behind the boundary. Swap Postgres for anything else and the service code never changes.
